meaning: "thorough and courteous," "very kind and attentive," or "careful and detailed (in explanation)."NuanceThis is a four-character compound (yojijukugo) that combines 懇切 (kind, solicitous, heartfelt) with 丁寧 (polite, careful). Together, it conveys the idea of someone taking extra care to be considerate and thorough, often in giving explanations, guidance, or service. It emphasizes both the warmth of concern (not just mechanical politeness) and the completeness of detail. Because of this, it’s often used positively in contexts like customer service, teaching, or writing instructions. The expression is formal, common in writing and polite speech, but less likely in casual conversation.Example Sentences先生は懇切丁寧に問題の解き方を説明してくれた。The teacher explained how to solve the problem thoroughly and kindly.懇切丁寧な対応のおかげで、安心して手続きを進めることができた。Thanks to the attentive and courteous assistance, I was able to proceed with the process confidently.彼の懇切丁寧な指導は、多くの生徒に感謝されている。His careful and considerate guidance is appreciated by many students

Superior (in rank/status/ability), a notch above, out of one's leagueNuance格上
 describes a person, organization, or object that is of a higher rank, 
status, grade, or ability compared to another. It implies a hierarchical
 relationship where one side is clearly positioned above the other. The 
"格" refers to social standing, rank, or class. This term is often used 
in competitive contexts (like sports or business), social hierarchies, 
or when comparing the quality of items. It carries a neutral to 
respectful tone, acknowledging the superior position or quality of the 
other party. It can also be used humbly to describe an opponent or goal 
that is "out of one's league."Example Sentences彼の実力は私より格上だ。His ability is a notch above mine.格上の大学に挑戦する。I will challenge myself by applying to a more prestigious university (one of a higher rank).あの会社は我が社より格上だ。That company is in a higher league than ours

Eating in advance; filling up now for later.Nuance:"食いだめ"
 is a colloquial term that literally combines "to eat" (食う) and "to 
store up" (溜め). It describes the act of eating a large meal in the 
present with the intention of staving off hunger for an extended period 
in the future, as if one were "stockpiling" satiety. This is often done 
when someone knows they will be busy or won't have access to food later.
 The word has a slightly rough or casual nuance and is not used in 
formal contexts. It can also be used humorously or figuratively.Example Sentences:昼にしっかり食いだめしておけば、夜は軽い食事で済む。If I fill up properly at lunch, a light meal will do for dinner.明日は忙しくなるから、今のうちに食いだめしておこう。Tomorrow will be busy, so I'll eat a big meal now to prepare.旅行前に食いだめするのは無意味だ。It's pointless to try and "eat in advance" before a trip

A sense of location; spatial awareness; knowing one's bearings.Nuance土地勘 (tochikan)
 refers to an intuitive understanding or sense of a geographical area, 
allowing one to navigate it without getting lost. It's the mental map 
one develops of a place. This "sense" is typically gained through 
direct, repeated experience in the area. The nuance is practical and 
instinctive; it's not just about knowing street names, but about feeling
 the layout and relationships between locations. Someone with good 土地勘 
can find shortcuts or reorient themselves quickly if they take a wrong 
turn. It's often used when this sense is either present or lacking.Example Sentencesこの辺りは土地勘がないので、道に迷いやすい。I have no sense of this area, so I容易 get lost.タクシーの運転手は町全体に土地勘がある。The taxi driver has a good sense of the entire town's layout.何度か訪れて、ようやくこの街に土地勘がついた。After visiting a few times, I've finally gotten my bearings in this city

In the prime of youth, full of youthful vigor, hot-bloodedNuance血気盛ん
 describes a state, typically associated with youth, where one is full 
of physical energy, passion, and spirit. The term 血気 (kekki) refers to 
"blood and spirit," implying raw, impulsive energy, and 盛ん (sakan) means
 "prosperous" or "vigorous." It captures the positive aspects of youth 
like enthusiasm and drive, but also often implies a lack of maturity, 
patience, and restraint that can lead to recklessness or impetuosity. 
It's a descriptive term that acknowledges the power of youth while 
subtly warning of its potential for unchecked behavior.Example Sentences彼は血気盛んな青年で、何にでも挑戦する意欲がある。He is a youth in his prime, full of eagerness to take on any challenge.血気盛んな頃は、よく無茶をしたものだ。When I was young and full of vigor, I often did reckless things.血気盛んな隊員たちをまとめるのは大変だ。Managing the hot-blooded, energetic team members is a difficult task.

To put one's life on the line; to work one's hardest.Nuance:"命張る"
 is a very strong and vivid idiomatic expression that means to exert so 
much effort that it feels as if one is staking their very life on the 
task. It goes far beyond ordinary hard work, implying a supreme, 
all-or-nothing level of dedication, resolve, and personal risk. The 
nuance is one of extreme passion, desperation, or a profound sense of 
responsibility. It is often used in contexts of protecting something 
invaluable, achieving a critical goal, or in situations of intense 
competition or danger.Example Sentences:このプロジェクトには命張って取り組むつもりだ。I intend to tackle this project as if my life depended on it.命張ってでも、わが子は守る。I will protect my child even if it costs me my life.命張って働いて、やっと家を買えた。I worked my absolute hardest and finally managed to buy a house

Self-taught method; one's own style; unconventional way.Nuance我流 (garyū)
 refers to a method, style, or technique that one has developed on their
 own, without formal training or adherence to established schools or 
traditions. The nuance can be either positive or negative. Positively, 
it implies originality, independence, and a unique personal approach. 
Negatively, it can suggest a lack of proper foundation, being unorthodox
 in a flawed way, or having developed bad habits due to the absence of 
formal instruction. The context determines whether it praises someone's 
individuality or criticizes their amateurish techniques.Example Sentences彼のギターの弾き方は完全な我流だ。His way of playing the guitar is completely self-taught.我流でプログラミングを学んだので、基礎が疎かになっている。Since I learned programming on my own, my fundamentals are weak.彼女の我流の経営術が、会社を成功に導いた。Her unique, self-developed management style led the company to success

To scatter, to fall apart, to come loose, to dissipateNuance散ける
 is the intransitive verb form meaning "to scatter" or "to become 
dispersed." It describes a state where things that were once together 
naturally come apart and spread out without a direct external force 
being applied. It can refer to physical objects, like petals falling 
from a flower, or to abstract things, like concentration dissipating or a
 group of people breaking up. The nuance is often passive and natural, 
implying a loss of cohesion or unity. It can also carry a poetic or 
melancholic tone, suggesting transience and fragility, such as in the 
image of scattered cherry blossoms.Example Sentences桜の花びらが風に散けていく。The cherry blossom petals scatter in the wind.話し声が聞こえて、勉強の集中力が散けてしまった。I heard voices, and my concentration on studying dissipated.チームの連携が散けて、試合に負けた。The team's coordination fell apart, and they lost the match

To be extraordinary; to be exceptional; to be out of the ordinary.Nuance:"並外れる"
 is a verb that describes a state of being far beyond the average or 
common standard, either in a positive or negative sense. It emphasizes a
 significant deviation from the norm. While it can be used for 
exceptional physical size, its most common usage is for extraordinary 
ability, talent, effort, or quality. The nuance is one of objective 
remarkableness, often with a tone of awe or surprise at the degree of 
the difference. It is a more formal and literary term than the adjective
 "並外れた".Example Sentences:彼は並外れた記憶力の持ち主だ。He possesses an extraordinary memory.その選手は並外れる身体能力を誇る。That athlete boasts exceptional physical abilities.彼女の成功は並外れた努力の結果である。Her success is the result of extraordinary effort

Travel souvenir story; tale of one's travels.Nuance土産話 (miyagebanashi)
 refers to the stories and experiences one brings back from a trip to 
share with those who stayed home. The word combines 土産 (souvenir/gift) 
and 話 (story). The nuance is one of sharing and entertainment; it's not 
just a dry report but an engaging narrative meant to convey the 
highlights, interesting encounters, and unique experiences of the 
journey. These stories are themselves considered a type of "souvenir" 
for the listeners, allowing them to partake in the traveler's adventures
 vicariously. It implies a sense of excitement and a desire to share 
one's experiences.Example Sentences海外出張から帰った父が、家族に土産話をした。My father, who returned from a business trip abroad, told us stories of his travels.彼女の北海道での土産話はとても面白かった。Her stories about her trip to Hokkaido were very interesting.何か良い土産話はありますか。Do you have any good travel stories?

Senile, dotageNuance耄碌
 is a term that describes a state of advanced mental and physical 
decline due to extreme old age, characterized by forgetfulness, 
confusion, and a general inability to care for oneself. It is a very 
direct, blunt, and now often considered derogatory or politically 
incorrect word. While it factually denotes senility, its usage can be 
seen as insensitive and disrespectful. In modern Japanese, more neutral 
and respectful terms like 認知症 (ninchishō - dementia) or ぼける (bokeru - to
 become senile, though still informal) are often preferred. 耄碌 carries a
 strong negative connotation of frailty and helplessness associated with
 the worst stereotypes of aging.Example Sentences彼はすっかり耄碌して、自分の子供の名前も忘れてしまった。He has become completely senile and even forgot his own children's names.あの教授もかつては偉大だったが、今では耄碌している。That professor was once great, but now he is in his dotage.耄碌した老人の面倒を見るのは大変な仕事だ。Taking care of a senile old person is a difficult task

Manners; etiquette; procedure; way of doing something.Nuance:"作法"
 has two primary layers of meaning. The first and most common refers to 
the formal rules of polite behavior and social etiquette, such as table 
manners or ceremonial conduct. The second refers to the proper method, 
procedure, or "way" of doing a specific activity, like the tea ceremony,
 calligraphy, or even a technical process. In both cases, the core 
nuance is a set of established, traditional forms that are considered 
correct and proper, often passed down through generations. It implies a 
respect for form and convention.Example Sentences:祖父は箸の作法にうるさい。My grandfather is strict about chopstick etiquette.茶道の作法を三年間習った。I studied the procedures of the tea ceremony for three years.このソフトウェアの正しい作法に従ってインストールしてください。Please install this software according to the correct procedure

Travel expenses; journey money; fare.Nuance路銀 (rogin)
 is a somewhat old-fashioned or literary term for money needed for a 
journey, specifically for transportation costs like train or bus fares, 
or for general travel expenses. The nuance is practical and slightly 
austere, evoking an image of having just enough coins or cash for the 
trip itself. It's not used for large, luxurious travel budgets but 
rather for the fundamental cost of getting from one place to another. 
While still understood, it is less common in modern daily conversation 
than the more general 旅費 (ryohi - travel expenses) or specific terms 
like 交通費 (kōtsūhi - transportation costs).Example Sentencesポケットに路銀を確かめてから家を出た。I checked that I had my fare in my pocket before leaving home.路銀もなくし、途方に暮れた。I lost my travel money and was at a complete loss.これが最後の路銀だ。This is my last bit of journey money

Present progressive formNuanceIn
 Japanese grammar, 現在進行形 refers specifically to the verb form that 
describes an ongoing action or a temporary state happening at the 
present moment. It is formed by using the て-form of a verb followed by 
いる (e.g., 食べている - "is eating"). The core nuance is that the action is in progress now.
 It can also be used to describe a continuous state resulting from a 
past action (e.g., 結婚している - "is married"). This grammatical term is 
neutral and technical, used for explaining language rules. It does not 
carry the metaphorical meaning of "something currently in progress" that
 the English phrase "present progressive" might have in casual 
conversation.Example Sentences「食べている」は、動詞「食べる」の現在進行形です。"食べている" is the present progressive form of the verb "食べる".

Conjecture, guess, perception, intuitionNuance察し
 refers to the ability to intuitively understand or guess another 
person's feelings, thoughts, or a situation without them being 
explicitly stated. It is a highly valued social skill in Japanese 
culture, where indirect communication is common. The term implies 
empathy, sensitivity, and the capacity to "read between the lines." A 
person with good 察し is considered attentive and considerate. The phrase 
察しが良い (sasshi ga ii) means "perceptive" or "quick on the uptake," while

understanding unspoken social cues.Example Sentences彼は私の気持ちを察して、何も聞かなかった。He guessed my feelings and didn't ask anything.お察しの通り、計画は失敗に終わりました。As you have likely surmised, the plan ended in failure.あの人は本当に察しが悪くて、いつも説明が必要だ。That person is really slow on the uptake and always needs everything explained

A wasted trip; a fruitless journey.Nuance:"無駄足"
 describes the experience of making a trip to a place for a specific 
purpose, only to find that the purpose cannot be fulfilled—because the 
person was not there, the place was closed, the item was sold out, etc. 
The nuance captures the frustration and futility of the effort expended 
in traveling. It emphasizes the wasted time and energy, and there is 
often an unspoken sense of disappointment or annoyance. It is a very 
common and practical term in everyday conversation.Example Sentences:店が休みだと知らずに行き、無駄足になった。I went without knowing the shop was closed, so it was a wasted trip.彼に会うために東京まで行ったが、留守で無駄足に終わった。I went all the way to Tokyo to see him, but he was out and it ended up being a fruitless journey.事前に電話すれば、無駄足を防げる。If you call ahead, you can avoid a wasted trip

Sake (alcohol) is the best of all medicines.Nuance酒は百薬の長 (sake wa hyakuyaku no chō)

that moderate consumption of alcohol is beneficial to health and can 
surpass all other medicines. The nuance is not an endorsement of heavy 
drinking but rather a cultural acknowledgment of alcohol's role in 
relaxation, socialization, and purported health benefits when consumed 
in small quantities. However, in modern contexts, it is often cited with

implicitly acknowledging the potential dangers of excess.Example Sentences「一杯どうだ？」「そうだな、酒は百薬の長と言うし」"How about a drink?" "Well, they do say sake is the best of all medicines."父はいつも「酒は百薬の長」と言いながら、晩酌を楽しんでいる。My father always enjoys his evening drink while saying, "sake is the best of all medicines."酒は百薬の長とは言うが、飲み過ぎは厳禁だ。While it's said that alcohol is the best of all medicines, overdrinking is strictly forbidden.

To be weak in the endgame; to lack follow-through; to be sloppy in the final stage.Nuance:"詰めが甘い"
 originates from board games like shogi and go, where it refers to a

describes a person who is careless or lacks thoroughness in the final 
stages of any task, project, or plan, often leading to avoidable 
mistakes or failure despite a strong start. It criticizes a lack of 
attention to detail, perseverance, or decisive action when finishing up,
 implying that the person becomes complacent or loses focus just before 
the goal is achieved.Example Sentences:彼はいつも詰めが甘く、最後でミスをしてしまう。He's always sloppy at the end and makes a mistake at the last moment.企画書は良かったが、プレゼンの詰めが甘かった。The proposal was good, but the follow-through in the presentation was weak.リードしていても、詰めが甘ければ負けることがある。Even if you're in the lead, you can still lose if your endgame is weak

Oral tradition, oral transmission, secret teachings passed down by word of mouthNuance口伝
 refers to knowledge, techniques, traditions, or secret teachings that 
are passed down directly from a master to a disciple through spoken 
word, rather than through written texts. It emphasizes a personal, 
direct, and often secretive or exclusive line of transmission. This 
method is common in traditional Japanese arts, crafts, and martial arts 
(e.g., 茶道, 武道) where subtle nuances, secrets, or spiritual aspects are 
considered too profound or complex to be fully captured in writing. The 
term carries a nuance of authenticity, tradition, and esoteric knowledge
 that is preserved within a specific lineage or school.Example Sentencesこの秘技は師匠からの口伝で伝えられている。This secret technique has been passed down through oral transmission from the master.和菓子作りの極意は、ほとんどが口伝である。The essence of traditional Japanese confectionery making is largely an oral tradition.彼は口伝によってのみ伝承される古い歌を覚えている。He remembers an old song that is only preserved through oral tradition

Unknown; undisclosed; not specified.Nuance:"不詳"
 is a formal term used to indicate that information is unknown, unclear,
 or deliberately not specified. It is commonly found in official 
documents, databases, encyclopedias, and news reports where a field of 
information is left blank or marked as unknown. The nuance is neutral 
and factual, simply stating the lack of available or relevant 
information. It does not carry the mystery or negativity of words like 
"怪しい" (suspicious); it is merely a statement of absence, often for 
bureaucratic or practical reasons.Example Sentences:この古文書の作者は不詳である。The author of this ancient document is unknown.事件の発生時刻は不詳とされている。The time of the incident is listed as unknown.資料には不詳と記入されている項目がある。There are fields in the document marked as "unknown."

A surprise night attack; an ambush; a stab in the back.Nuance闇討ち (yamiuchi)
 literally means "attacking in the darkness of night." Historically, it 
referred to a military tactic of a surprise assault under cover of 
darkness. In modern usage, it retains its core meaning of a treacherous,
 unexpected attack but is used more broadly and figuratively. It 
describes any underhanded, deceitful action where someone is assaulted 
(physically, socially, or in business) without warning or a chance to 
defend themselves, akin to a "stab in the back." The nuance is strongly 
negative, emphasizing the cowardice, treachery, and unfairness of the 
assailant.Example Sentences敵軍は夜明け前に闇討ちを仕掛けてきた。The enemy forces launched a surprise night attack just before dawn.あの批判は完全な闇討ちだ。前もって何の警告もなかった。That criticism is a complete ambush. There was no warning beforehand.ビジネスの世界では、闇討ちのようなやり方は信用を失う。In the business world, underhanded methods like backstabbing will make you lose trust

Revenge, retaliation, paying back in kind, settling a scoreNuance意趣返し
 is a term for revenge that carries a specific nuance of repaying a past
 wrong or insult in a manner that is fitting and poetic, often mirroring
 the original offense. The word 意趣 (ishi) implies a "grudge" or 
"resentment" stemming from a personal slight or injustice. Unlike simple
 revenge, 意趣返し suggests a calculated and deliberate act to restore one's
 honor or pride by making the offender experience a similar humiliation 
or loss. It often has a dramatic, almost narrative quality, implying 
that the retaliation is not just about harm but about poetic justice and
 settling a personal score.Example Sentences彼は過去の侮辱に対する意趣返しとして、相手の失敗を公然と嘲笑した。As revenge for a past insult, he publicly mocked his opponent's failure.これは単なる競争ではなく、昔の恨みに対する意趣返しだ。This isn't just competition; it's payback for an old grudge.ついに長年の意趣返しを果たした。He finally got his long-awaited revenge

Concealment; hiding; suppression.Nuance:"隠匿"
 refers to the deliberate and active act of hiding something, such as 
information, evidence, or assets, to prevent its discovery. The term 
carries a strong negative and legalistic connotation, often implying 
that the act is unethical, illegal, or done with malicious intent. It is
 commonly used in contexts of scandal, crime, corruption, or legal 
proceedings, where someone is accused of concealing the truth. The 
nuance is one of secrecy and deception for personal or organizational 
gain.Example Sentences:会社は重要な情報を隠匿した疑いで調査されている。The company is under investigation for allegedly concealing important information.彼は資産を隠匿して脱税した。He hid his assets and evaded taxes.証拠隠匿の罪で起訴された。He was indicted on charges of suppressing evidence

Funeral procession; burial; internment; seeing off the deceased.Nuance葬送 (sōsō)
 refers to the formal act and ceremony of conveying the deceased to 
their final resting place, encompassing the entire funeral procession 
and burial/cremation rites. The nuance is solemn, respectful, and 
ritualistic, focusing on the communal act of escorting the dead on their
 final journey. It carries a weight of tradition, finality, and social 
duty. While it can be used in a straightforward, descriptive way, it 
often evokes a somber and poignant atmosphere, marking the physical and 
symbolic separation of the deceased from the world of the living.Example Sentences多くの人が故人の葬送に参列した。Many people attended the funeral procession of the deceased.静かな葬送の列が墓地へと向かった。A quiet funeral procession made its way to the cemetery.彼の葬送は質素に行われた。His burial was conducted in a simple manner

Thoughtless, hasty, rash, imprudentNuance短慮
 is a noun that describes a state of mind characterized by a lack of 
deep thought, foresight, or careful consideration. It implies that a 
person's thinking is "short" (短) and fails to consider the broader 
context, long-term consequences, or complexities of a situation. This 
leads to hasty decisions, rash judgments, or imprudent actions. The term
 is critical and carries a negative connotation, suggesting that the 
person is impulsive and unable to think things through properly. It is 
often used to admonish someone for a careless mistake or a poorly 
planned action.Example Sentences彼の短慮が大きな問題を引き起こした。His thoughtlessness caused a major problem.短慮を謝罪した。He apologized for his rashness.そんな短慮な行動は慎むべきだ。You should refrain from such imprudent actions

A direct appeal (to a higher authority); bypassing the chain of command.Nuance:"直訴"
 refers to the act of appealing directly to the highest person in 
authority (like a shogun, lord, or CEO), bypassing all intermediate 
levels of management or bureaucracy. Historically, this was often a 
desperate and dangerous act, sometimes involving stopping a lord's 
procession. The term carries a strong nuance of desperation, urgency, 
and a breakdown of normal channels. It implies that the matter is so 
critical that the petitioner is willing to risk severe punishment for 
the breach of protocol to be heard. In modern use, it retains this sense
 of a dramatic, last-resort appeal.Example Sentences:農民たちは年貢の減免を将軍に直訴した。The peasants made a direct appeal to the shogun for a reduction in their annual tax.部下からの直訴によって、部長の不正が明らかになった。The department manager's misconduct was revealed by a direct appeal from a subordinate.彼は社長に直訴するという危険を冒した。He took the risk of making a direct appeal to the company president

Reconciliation; making peace; rapprochement.Nuance和睦 (waboku)
 refers to the act of ending a conflict or dispute and restoring 
peaceful, friendly relations between two opposing parties, such as 
nations, families, or individuals. The nuance is formal and significant,
 implying the resolution of a serious, often prolonged conflict. It 
suggests a mutual agreement to cease hostilities and is commonly used in
 historical or diplomatic contexts. Unlike a simple truce, 和睦 carries a 
stronger sense of restored harmony and settled differences, often

Taking out the trash, garbage disposalNuanceゴミ出し

 that are visibly or structurally integral to the final product. It is

vegetables, meat) in a dish, as opposed to seasonings or broth. It can

Eunuch; court castrato.Nuance:"宦官"

Austerities; ascetic practices; penance.Nuance:"苦行"

Hairpin; hair ornament.Nuance簪 (kanzashi)

Skinny; slender; lean.Nuance:"痩せぎす"

Sleepwalking; somnambulism.Nuance夢遊病 (muyūbyō)

Design; pattern.Nuance:"図案"

nuance of deliberate, artistic planning rather than a spontaneous sketch

The art of unspoken communication; conveying one's will without words; intuitive understanding (often through the hara/gut).Nuance腹芸 (haragei)

Archaeological find, excavated artifactNuance出土品

civilizations. It carries a formal and academic nuance, directly 
associating the object with the field of archaeology and the process of 
discovery. These items are typically studied to understand ancient human
 activity and are often housed in museums or research institutions.Example Sentencesこの土器は縄文時代の出土品だ。This pottery is an archaeological find from the Jomon period.遺跡から多くの貴重な出土品が発見された。Many valuable artifacts were discovered at the archaeological site.出土品の分析から、当時の生活様式が明らかになった。The analysis of the excavated artifacts revealed the lifestyle of that time

Full of holes; sparse; not filled; hollow.Nuance:"スカスカ"

content. It evokes a sense of emptiness and insubstantiality.Example Sentences:このセーターは編み目がスカスカだ。This sweater is loosely knitted (full of holes).鞄の中身がスカスカなので、本を何冊か入れよう。The bag is mostly empty, so I'll put a few books in it.今月のスケジュールはスカスカだ。My schedule for this month is wide open (sparse)

To shift; to change; to transition; to be transient.Nuance移ろう (utsurou)
 describes a gradual, natural, and often subtle change or transition,

impermanent nature of the world. Unlike the more general 変わる (kawaru - 
to change), 移ろう focuses on the process of transformation itself, evoking

and aesthetic contexts to capture the beautiful but transient essence of

"ordinary," "run-of-the-mill," or "commonplace."Nuance:This slightly archaic term dismisses something as unremarkably average—often used with a tone of weary familiarity.Example Sentences:凡百の作家とは一線を画す。("He stands apart from run-of-the-mill writers.")凡百な意見は聞き飽きた。("I’m tired of hearing commonplace opinions.")凡百の企業では面白くない。("Working for an ordinary company wouldn’t be interesting.")

憤る（いきどおる）means "to be indignant," "to

visceral reaction to perceived injustice or wrongdoing.Nuance:This term implies moral outrage—a
 fiery, often articulate anger driven by principle. Unlike 怒る (general 
anger), 憤る suggests the anger is socially or ethically charged (e.g., 
toward corruption, inequality).Example Sentences:不正行為を知り、胸が憤る思いだった。(Learning of the fraud, I felt my chest tighten with indignation.)彼は社会の不条理に憤る活動家だ。(He’s an activist who rails against societal absurdities.)弱い者いじめを見て、思わず憤ってしまった。(Watching the bullying of the vulnerable, I couldn’t help but seethe.)Note: Often used in political or philosophical contexts. Related term: 憤慨（ふんがい, "righteous fury").

Translation:しゃしゃり出る (shasharideru) – To push oneself forward obtrusively; to intrude where not welcome (like a photo-bomber in a group picture).Example Sentences:彼はいつも会議にしゃしゃり出て、余計な意見を言う。(He always intrudes into meetings to offer unnecessary opinions.)先輩の話に後輩がしゃしゃり出てきて空気が悪くなった。(A junior butted into the seniors’ conversation, killing the mood.)親の議論に子供がしゃしゃり出てきた。(The child meddled obtrusively in the adults’ discussion.)Memorable Tip:The word’s “しゃしゃり” mimics the sound of shuffling feet dragging forward intrusively.  phrase carries a sense of urgency or inevitability, often implying that
 something is so critical it cannot be ignored or postponed. It can also
 suggest a matter of great importance, sometimes with a formal or 
dramatic tone. The term is often used in contexts where delay or 
inaction is not an option.Example Sentences:この問題は止ん事無いので、すぐに対処しなければならない。(This issue is urgent and must be addressed immediately.)彼の提案は止ん事無いもので、全員が賛成した。(His proposal was absolutely necessary, and everyone agreed.)止ん事無い用事ができて、会議を途中で抜けなければならなかった。(An unavoidable matter came up, and I had to leave the meeting early.)止ん事無い（やんごとない）indeed has a secondary meaning of "elegant" or "of high status" (often referring to nobility or refined things), in addition to its primary sense of "inevitable/unavoidable."Primary Meaning ("Inevitable"):Used in urgent contexts where something cannot be overlooked (e.g., critical duties, emergencies).Example: 止ん事無い用事 (urgent business that cannot wait).Secondary Meaning ("Elegant/High-class"):Derives from the idea that certain matters/people are too elevated to be ignored (e.g., nobility, exquisite items).Example: やんごとなきお方 (a person of high rank/elegance).Example Sentences (Elegance Meaning):彼女はやんごとなき家柄の出身だ。(She comes from an aristocratic family.)パーティーにはやんごとなき品々が並んだ。(The party displayed exquisite, high-class items.)あの店はやんごとない客しか入れない。(That store only admits high-society clients.)Example Sentences (Inevitable Meaning):これは止ん事無い問題だ、即座に対処せよ。(This is an unavoidable issue—address it immediately.)止ん事無い用事で遅刻した。(I was late due to pressing business.)

Nuance:
大立ち回り originally comes from Kabuki theater, where it referred to an elaborate, choreographed sword-fighting scene—the kind that’s flashy and dramatic. In modern usage, it can still refer to stage combat, but it’s also used figuratively to describe a big fuss, loud quarrel, or heated confrontation, often involving exaggerated or theatrical behavior. It carries a dramatic, attention-grabbing tone, sometimes humorous or critical.

Wandering; drifting; being tossed about; a sense of withering or falling (like leaves).
Nuance: A classical/literary expression of Chinese origin, not common in modern spoken Japanese. It evokes an image of being at the mercy of the wind—leaves scattering, a person wandering with no place to settle, or a life marked by transience and instability. Example Sentences:

戦乱の世にあって、多くの人々が飄零を余儀なくされた。

 – To praise extravagantly; to celebrate; to hold someone/something in

"sympathetic crying," or "tearing up in response to someone else's tears."Nuances:This term describes an empathic, involuntary reaction—seeing

 moments.Example Sentences:彼女の卒業スピーチにもらい泣きした。(I cried along with her graduation speech.)ドラマの感動的なシーンでついもらい泣きしてしまった。(I couldn’t help but cry along with the touching scene in the drama.)友人の苦労話を聞き、もらい泣きする人が多かった。(Many people shed sympathetic tears hearing my friend’s hardships.)

blatant; shameless; feigned; too obvious

そんな白々しい言い訳は通用しない。

Cheerful and lighthearted; in high spiritsNuances:This
 onomatopoeic term describes a buoyant, happy mood where one feels like 
skipping or humming. It carries connotations of carefree joy and

 specific than 嬉しい (happy), ルンルン suggests visible, almost physical

paints a picture of someone so happy they might literally be humming a

A coaxing voice; a syrupy sweet voice; "cat-petting voice"Nuances:This
 term describes an artificially sweet, flattering, or coaxing tone of 
voice someone uses to get what they want—comparable to how one might

The expression implies:The speaker is being disingenuously sweetThey're trying to manipulate or persuadeThe tone feels unnatural and calculatedWhile
 sometimes used playfully between partners, it's often 
critical—suggesting the speaker is being transparently manipulative. 
It's that cloying, honeyed tone people use when they want something from
 you.

 refers to the act of purchasing goods, typically in bulk or on a

transaction, often involving negotiation, and is commonly used in

 in some other systems. In a literal sense, it denotes a mid-level

 implying they are a "nobody" or a "piece of trash." The term carries a

Violent/serious – Euphemistic expression for killing someone with one's own hands—used in dramatic, literary, or emotional situations.


Practical – Handling or working on something personally, rather than delegating it.



Example Sentences:


この花は私が手にかけて育てたんです。

愛する人を自分の手にかけるなんて、耐えられない。

社長自らがこのプロジェクトに手にかけている。

assets, documents, or goods) to a person or an institution for 
safekeeping or management. It implies a contractual or formal 
arrangement where the recipient (the trustee) has a clear responsibility
 to protect and manage the item, but the ownership remains with the 
person who deposited it. It is more formal and specific than the common

Mostly seen in novels, poetry, or dramatic descriptions rather than daily speech.

 kanji 奮 (stir/exert) + 起 (rise) vividly depicts "stirring oneself to 
rise up." It implies a turning point where one shakes off lethargy or 
defeatism and actively engages with a challenge. Often used in contexts 
of competition, personal development, or overcoming adversity, it 
suggests a powerful, internal mobilization of spirit and will.

Eventually; In the future; In the long run
Nuance:
行く行く is an adverbial expression that conveys the idea of something happening down the line, over time, or eventually. While the word literally repeats “to go,” its idiomatic use implies the gradual passage of time leading to a particular state or outcome — similar to "someday" or "in due course" in English.

行く行くは自分の店を持ちたいと思っている。
Eventually, I hope to have my own shop.


行く行く彼がリーダーになることは間違いないだろう。

Implies:Social shame in clingingEmotional immaturityBreach of stoic idealsDiffers

Translation:忠実（ちゅうじつ）means "faithful," "loyal," or "accurate," while 忠実しい（ちゅうじつしい） is an incorrect/archaic form—the proper adjective is 忠実な.Nuance:忠実: Neutral, used for people (loyalty), translations (accuracy), or machines (precise operation).忠実しい: A rare, outdated variant occasionally seen in classical literature (not used in modern Japanese).Example Sentences (Correct Usage):彼は会社に忠実な従業員だ。(He is a loyal employee to the company.)この翻訳は原文に忠実である。(This translation is faithful to the original text.)ロボットは命令に忠実に動いた。(The robot moved precisely according to instructions.)Note: Stick to 忠実な in modern contexts. extreme measure; daring trick; drastic action; bold technique
Nuance: 荒業 refers to an extraordinary, often risky or unconventional method used to achieve a goal. It can apply to physical feats (in martial arts, performance, or stunts) or to bold strategies in other contexts. The nuance emphasizes daring, audacity, and sometimes recklessness.
Example sentences:


彼は荒業で危機を乗り越えた。
He overcame the crisis with a daring move.


手品師は観客を驚かせるために荒業を披露した。
The magician performed a bold trick to astonish the audience.


時には荒業に出るしかない状況もある。
Sometimes, there’s no choice but to resort to extreme measures

意地を張る（いじをはる）means "to stubbornly insist
 on one's own way," "to be obstinate," or "to dig in one's heels." It 
describes an inflexible attitude, often despite reason or consequences.Nuance:This phrase carries a negative connotation,
 implying childish or selfish rigidity. Unlike 信念を貫く (to stick to 
principles), 意地を張る suggests pointless defiance driven by pride.Example Sentences:彼は意地を張って謝ろうとしない。(He’s being stubborn and refuses to apologize.)意地を張らずに、仲直りしたほうがいい。(Stop being obstinate and just make up already.)母は意地を張って、助けを求めるのを拒んだ。(My mother stubbornly refused to ask for help.)Note: Often used with criticism (e.g., 意地を張るな！ = "Don’t be so pigheaded!"). 形式的（けいしきてき）means "formal," "pro forma,"
 or "perfunctory." It refers to actions or behaviors done for the sake 
of adhering to procedure or appearance, often lacking genuine intent or 
substance.Nuance:This
 term often carries a slightly negative connotation, implying that 
something is done superficially or mechanically without real meaning or 
enthusiasm. It can suggest rigidity or hollow compliance with rules.Example Sentences:彼の謝罪はまったく形式的で、誠意が感じられなかった。(His apology was purely pro forma, with no sense of sincerity.)会議での承認は形式的なもので、実際の決定はすでに終わっていた。(The approval in the meeting was just a formality—the real decision had already been made.)形式的な挨拶だけで、中身のある話し合いはできなかった。(We only exchanged perfunctory greetings and couldn’t have a meaningful discussion.)

埒があかない (らちがあかない) means "to make no progress," "to be stuck in limbo," or "to remain unresolved." It describes a situation that drags on endlessly without resolution or forward movement.Example Sentences:議論が埒があかず、結論が出ない。(The debate goes in circles with no conclusion.)上司の承認が得られず、プロジェクトは埒があかない状態だ。(Without the boss’s approval, the project is in limbo.)埒があかないから、強硬手段に出た。(Since it was going nowhere, we took drastic measures.)Memorable Tip:埒 (enclosure/gate) + あかない (won’t open) → "the gate won’t budge." Picture a "stuck door" blocking progress. Often used for bureaucratic delays.

折しも（おりしも）means "just at that moment," 
"coincidentally," or "as it happens." It highlights a timely or fateful 
coincidence, often in narratives.Nuance:This literary term adds dramatic weight to timing—unlike ちょうど (exactly), 折しも implies the moment is meaningful or opportune. Common in formal writing or speeches.Example Sentences:折しも空が暗くなり、雨が降り出した。(Just at that moment, the sky darkened and rain began.)彼が到着したのは、折しも会議が始まるときだった。(He arrived just as the meeting was starting—as if timed.)折しもそのニュースが世界を駆け巡った。(As fate would have it, that news spread across the globe.)Note: Often paired with ～とき or ～瞬間. Rare in casual speech; replaces たまたま in elevated contexts.

狭心症（きょうしんしょう）means "angina pectoris," a medical condition characterized by chest pain due to reduced blood flow to the heart.Nuance:This clinical term implies intermittent, ischemic pain—unlike 心筋梗塞 (heart attack), 狭心症 is typically temporary but signals coronary artery disease. Requires urgent attention.Example Sentences:階段を上ると狭心症の症状が出る。(Climbing stairs triggers my angina symptoms.)狭心症の予防には生活習慣の改善が不可欠だ。(Lifestyle changes are vital to prevent angina.)ニトログリセリンは狭心症の発作を緩和する。(Nitroglycerin alleviates angina attacks.)Note: Often abbreviated as 狭心. Contrast with 不整脈（ふせいみゃく, "arrhythmia").

The nuance is stronger than simply being tired or tipsy—it implies being completely overcome, with judgment and perception shut down. "just in case" approach to luck.

Tree felling; logging; cutting down treesNuances:This
 term specifically refers to the act of cutting down trees, often in a 
planned or industrial context (like forestry or construction). Unlike

and is commonly used in environmental, agricultural, or construction 
discussions.Example Sentences:この山林では、許可なく伐採を行うことは禁止されている。(In this mountain forest, unauthorized tree felling is prohibited.)伐採された木材は、近くの製材所へ運ばれた。(The felled timber was transported to a nearby sawmill.)環境保護のため、違法伐採を取り締まる法律が強化された。(To protect the environment, laws against illegal logging have been strengthened.)Nuance Note:Often
 appears in debates about deforestation (森林伐採) or sustainable forestry.
